submission.natural_language_explanation: N2748+ is a retrospective token-identity detector, not a context or next-token feature: the peak sits on the word at the current position (zeroing layer 1's attention output leaves 60-90% of it, and the same word shifts by well under a third across different preceding and following text), near neighbours of a firing word also fire (their mean is 0.17 against 0.01 for the vocabulary at large), and the rest of the vocabulary sits at 0. It fires on a broad, graded, lexically specific set of everyday content words centred on three clusters - commerce and media nouns (firm, firms, brand, brands, market, markets, shares, ownership, ads, commercials, logo, auction, wholesale, publisher, studio, news, press), consumer-goods nouns (diaper, diapers, pants, jeans, trousers, shoes, stove, underwear) and evaluative degree adverbs (exclusively, constantly, increasingly, suddenly, rightfully, firmly, forcefully, entirely, continually, actively, totally, completely) - and it stays silent on function words, on abstract or technical Latinate vocabulary (method, process, analysis, system, information), on neutral objects, places and organisations (water, house, car, road, tree, city, school, company, group, product, report, retail) and on manner and hedging adverbs (quickly, carefully, probably, generally, apparently); the boundary is lexical rather than conceptual, so exact word form and case decide the outcome - 'firm' 0.80 vs 'group' 0.00 and 'Falls' 0.69 vs 'falls' 0.02 in the same sentence, 'exclusively' 0.60 vs 'solely' 0.00 - and a new word should be labelled predicted-active only when it falls inside those three neighbourhoods.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The high street in Ashbourne has changed a good deal in twenty years. When I was a boy there were four butchers, a bakery, two greengrocers and a hardware store where you could buy nails by weight. Today only the bakery survives, and even that is run by a family who drive in from the next county every morning.

The buildings are mostly unchanged. The council repainted the railings outside the old corn exchange, and somebody has planted limes along the pavement where the benches used to be. On Saturdays the square fills with stalls selling honey, cheese and second-hand tools, and the queue for the fish van stretches past the war memorial.

What has really altered is how people buy. Most households order online and have the boxes left at the door, so delivery vans come and go all morning. The two remaining grocers say their takings fell by a third in five years, though they still know every customer by name and will keep a parcel behind the counter until you collect it. The owner of the hardware store says he earns more from repairs now than from the stock on his shelves.

There is talk of turning the empty unit beside the bank into a cafe. The planning papers went in during March and nobody objected. Whether it thrives is another question; the last three tenants lasted less than a year between them. Still, on a warm evening the street looks much as it must have done in 1950, and the children cycling up and down it do not seem to notice what is missing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
We moved into the flat in September, three weeks before the baby was due, and spent the first fortnight painting the small room at the back. The flat was on the second floor of a converted house near the canal, with a narrow staircase and a boiler that complained all winter. The landlord had promised new windows but sent a man to look at them twice and nothing else happened. We hung a curtain over the gap where the sash would not close and hoped the winter would be mild.

The hospital bag sat by the door for eleven days. My mother-in-law rang every evening to ask whether anything had started, and I learned to answer in a way that ended the conversation quickly without being rude. We had bought a second-hand cot from a couple in Chorlton and it took two evenings and most of a toolbox to put together.

When it finally happened it was four in the morning and the streets were empty. The taxi took twenty minutes to arrive and the driver, a patient man from Leeds, kept telling us to breathe. By six we were in a room with a window facing a car park, and by ten it was over. She weighed six pounds and four ounces and had a great deal of dark hair.

The first weeks are a blur of small logistics. I learned to change a nappy on my knee, to warm a bottle with one hand while holding a telephone with the other, and to sleep in twenty-minute pieces. The woman in the flat below complained twice about the noise, then came up with a tin of biscuits and apologised, and after that she would sometimes take the pram out for an hour so that we could rest.

What surprised me was the shopping. Nobody warns you how much of it there is. We were ordering diapers by the case, wipes by the box, and a delivery of formula every ten days, and still the cupboard beside the washing machine was never quite full. In the sixth week I finally sat down and listed everything we actually used, and it was shorter than I expected.

By spring she was sleeping until five and the flat felt larger. We took the curtain down when the windows were finally replaced, and the room at the back filled with light. I still keep the list in a drawer; it seems now like a record of a different person.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'diapers' from the consumer-goods cluster buried deep inside a long first-person passage in a genre absent from the examples, testing that the claimed word form fires even when it sits far into an unrelated document.

It fires on a broad, graded, lexically specific set of everyday content words centred on three clusters - commerce and media nouns (firm, firms, brand, brands, market, markets, shares, ownership, ads, commercials, logo, auction, wholesale, publisher, studio, news, press), consumer-goods nouns (diaper, diapers, pants, jeans, trousers, shoes, stove, underwear) and evaluative degree adverbs (exclusively, constantly, increasingly, suddenly, rightfully, firmly, forcefully, entirely, continually, actively, totally, completely) - and it stays silent on function words, on abstract or technical Latinate vocabulary (method, process, analysis, system, information), on neutral objects, places and organisations (water, house, car, road, tree, city, school, company, group, product, report, retail) and on manner and hedging adverbs (quickly, carefully, probably, generally, apparently); the boundary is lexical rather than conceptual, so exact word form and case decide the outcome - 'firm' 0.80 vs 'group' 0.00 and 'Falls' 0.69 vs 'falls' 0.02 in the same sentence, 'exclusively' 0.60 vs 'solely' 0.00 - and a new word should be labelled predicted-active only when it falls inside those three neighbourhoods.
